defects.description: The scoliotic curve is drawn as one step-shift, not a gentle S. The column runs almost straight from the base of the neck (0.23,0.556) through the racerback junction to about x0.54, jogs toward the near flank between x0.55 and x0.62, then runs straight to the waistband (0.82,0.633). The upper segment sits about midway across the visible back, but the lumbar segment sits about 69% of the way toward her near (left) flank and never comes back to the midline at the pelvis. A chiropractor would read it as a lateral shift rather than an S-curve. Not gross: the column stays on the back, in back view, along the body axis.

The overlay starts at the base of the neck (cervical and upper thoracic included), but the brief asked for the mid and lower back only. There are still about 22 vertebral units between the shoulders (x0.345) and the waistband, against 17 for T1-L5. That is down from about 26, and the count alone is not a fail item.

notes: Forearm elongation is fixed. Shoulder about x0.25, elbow about (0.67,0.80) with a clear olecranon depression, wrist about x0.96. Upper arm about 856 px and forearm about 600 px (ratio about 0.70), with the wrist reaching just past the waistband as expected. No rib cage is drawn any more; the leftover vertebra count is logged above. Her far (right) arm is hidden behind her torso, which is plausible at this camera height. Legs in leggings leave the right edge; no bare feet in frame. The red glow covers the paraspinal muscles around the bend, under the practitioner's left hand (about 0.52-0.73, 0.48-0.67). Practitioner face is out of frame (top edge shows shirt buttons only); patient face partly visible in the cradle (allowed). Left background device has a blank, blurred screen and the right shelf holds a physical spine model; no readable text. The left window area is posterized (render artifact common to this batch, outside the checklist). Pair pick: b.

defects.description: The practitioner's LEFT hand has no arm of its own. His left forearm comes out of the rolled cuff at about (0.30,0.20) and disappears behind the patient's LEFT trapezius/neck at about (0.415,0.275). The hand then reappears on the far side, cupping the patient's RIGHT shoulder, with its wrist hidden in front of it. Joining them needs about 0.30 of the frame (about 600 px) of hidden forearm across the front of the patient's neck. That implies a cuff-to-wrist forearm of about 0.43 of the frame, well over 1.5x a normal forearm against the patient's head size. It reads as a detached, extra hand on the shoulder. The strict rule (every hand must connect to its own arm; no over-long limbs) makes this a FAIL.

Right scapula is oversized and too medial. Its medial border sits at about x0.485-0.495, touching the drawn spine column (x0.457-0.495) instead of lying about 5-7 cm lateral to it. It spans about y0.336-0.645, roughly 1.6x a normal scapula height against the shoulder width. The faint left scapula shows the same size. Not gross: correct side, back-view orientation and shoulder-joint attachment.
